newsitem.title: UK: Dollar ends firmer in Europe as G7 and Fed eyed.
newsitem.headline: Dollar ends firmer in Europe as G7 and Fed eyed.

text.p: The dollar set a new four-year high against the yen and probed back above 1.65 marks in Europe on Tuesday as meetings of the Group of Seven industrial nations (G7) and the Federal Reserve helped underpin the U.S. unit.
G7 finance ministers meet Saturday in Berlin and official comments ahead of the meeting suggest they will broadly endorse the recent rise of the dollar while shunning excess volatility.

The Federal Open Market Committee met for the second day today, meantime. While no change in interest rates is expected, the outside chance of a rate rise has kept traders from pushing the dollar two far from recent ranges.

"The dollar is basically just idling around the place, with a degree of nervousness about the Fed, G7 and the January (U.S.) payrolls keeping it buoyed up," said Lee Ferridge, currency strategist at Commerzbank.
Ferridge said surprisingly weak German industrial orders data today and expectations of a weak January German unemployment report early tomorrow kept a lid on the mark.

At 1620 GMT, the dollar was trading at 1.6463/73 marks compared with 1.6464/69 late Tuesday and a intraday high at 1.6520. Against the yen, it was 123.33 compared with 122.43 on Tuesday and a new four-year high today at 123.52.
German December industrial orders fell 1.4 percent, lower than the 0.8 percent drop expected and throwing cold water on more robust December production data out yesterday.
The German January unemployment rate, meantime, is expected to rise to an 11.0 percent rate from 10.7 percent in December.
"The unemployment release for January will be far worse than expected," said Hans-Guenter Redeker, analyst at Chase Investment Bank.
Redeker cited German radio reports today which suggest a rise of 103,000 jobless, twice the consensus forecast for a 50,000 rise.
Several G7 players made statements ahead of the weekend meeting.
Japanese minister of finance Hiroshi Mitsuzuka said Japan will call for stability in exchange rates, downplaying recent scattered speculation it may look for a weaker dollar.
French president Jacques Chirac said France was benefiting from the current rise in the dollar, "which is gradually finding its normal level."
German finance minister Theo Waigel said he was happy with the dollar's rise and "we should be satisfied." IMF chief Michel Camdessus said the dollar move shows belief in U.S. economy.
Attention in Europe was on the growing debate about the timing of Italy and Spain's membership of the single European currency.

A report in today's Financial Times said a plan had already been hatched by the European Union to admit Italy to European monetary union (EMU) in 2000 or 2001, but not at the scheduled January 1, 1999 start date.

Although the lira and peseta weakened initially, they both staged impressive bounces and ended stronger on the day against the mark. All countries concerned, including Germany, said they were unaware of any such plan being agreed.

"The market initially read this report negatively but when people stood back a bit they realised that a firm compromise on Italy's entry date would lessen the chance of a big blow-out around 1998/1999," said Ferridge at Commerzbank.

Sterling powered ahead in the background, setting a 52-month high against the yen and popping back above 2.70 marks in late trading. Dealers cited several influences for the renewed sterling appetite, among them switching into UK government bonds from European and yen bonds. The Bank of England left interest rates unchanged today after the monthly UK monetary meeting.
--Mike Dolan, London newsroom +44 171 542 6762
